Micah 5:1 (4:14) also serves as a bridge text to the final you saying (5:2–4[1–3]) that begins in the next verse and concludes the second group of sayings that structures chapters 4–5. The end of 5:1 (4:14) introduces the theme of the role of the king, a topic that continues in 5:2–4(1–3).





5. “You” Will See a New Ruler (5:2–4[1–3])


5:2(1) With 5:2(1), a new addressee signals the passage’s shift into the final section of the second group of sayings in Mic 4–5.38 Micah 5:2(1) leaves behind the direct address of Lady Zion and its second-person feminine singular terms that identify Lady Zion as the primary addressee in 4:8b–5:1. Rather, 5:2 returns to the second-person masculine singular form of you that began the second group of sayings in 4:8.

The verse identifies the second-person masculine singular addressee as Bethlehem. Bethlehem lies approximately six miles south of Jerusalem. It is famous as the hometown of David and the place where Samuel went at Yahweh’s command to anoint David as king (1 Sam 16:1, 4; cf. 17:12). Ephrathah appears to be considered a leading clan of Bethlehem, tracing its roots back to Caleb, according to genealogical material in Chronicles (1 Chr 2:19, 50). Ephrathah is also associated with Davidic tradition since he is not only mentioned as an Ephrathite (1 Sam 17:12; cf. Ps 132:6), but the book of Ruth also associates Ephrathah with ancestors of David through Naomi and her dead husband Elimelech, along with Boaz and Ruth the Moabitess (Ruth 1:2; 4:11). One tradition even identifies Ephrathah as an earlier name for Bethlehem (Gen 35:19).

The last half of 5:2(1) makes two important claims: (1) that someone will go forth from Bethlehem to rule on Yahweh’s behalf, and (2) that this ruler’s origins go back to the distant past. The divine commission receives special emphasis when addressing Bethlehem. Despite the city’s seeming insignificance, Yahweh announces a new ruler will go forth from the city, and the announcement stresses both that he comes from Bethlehem and that Yahweh commissions him by putting two prepositional phrases side by side before the verb, linking the two ideas in rapid succession: from you for me he will go forth. The text alludes to the life of David in a manner that is consistent with the presentation of David’s rise in Samuel that recounts his anointing (1 Sam 16:1–13) at Yahweh’s insistence in Bethlehem and his taking of the city of Jerusalem to establish a dynasty in the “city of David” (2 Sam 5–7; see esp. 5:6–9; 7:11–12).

The reference to the distant past emphasizes the continuing hope for a Davidic ruler. Yahweh is the speaker, and significantly, Yahweh essentially affirms that this ancient promise has not ceased. The next ruler, like David, will come from Bethlehem and his origins go back into perpetuity. This phrasing links the future leader with the past in a way that can only imply a continuation of the Davidic promise that one of David’s descendants would sit on the throne into perpetuity (2 Sam 7:12–13).

12When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. 13He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. (NRSV)

Several commentators note, however, that the phrasing of this verse notably downplays two important elements of this royal promise. It avoids any reference to Jerusalem, and it does not refer to the future ruler as king. For them, the phrasing must be understood as intentional on both counts. By alluding to David’s origins as insignificant among the clans of Judah, the statement avoids any association with Jerusalem and the sins of its leaders.39 By avoiding naming this ruler “king,” this phrasing avoids anything that gets in the way of remembering that Yahweh is king, not a human who only acts as his agent.40 These astute observations should not be overlooked, but simultaneously, one must bear in mind that these are subtle connotations at best. The rhetorical aim of the passage primarily offers hope in the continuity of Davidic leadership for all Israelites. Yes, returning to Bethlehem avoids the association with the sins of past Davidic kings, but Yahweh still expects the ruler to go forth from there. Such subtle nuances would not change expectations that this new ruler would return to Jerusalem. The promise language in 2 Sam 7 tied the promise of Davidic rule to the promise of building a house in Jerusalem. In 2 Sam 7:12–13, the house of David and the house of Yahweh are bound together into perpetuity, when Yahweh promises as much to David:

12When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. 13He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. (NRSV)

By announcing Yahweh has appointed a new ruler with Davidic lineage, Mic 5:2(1) taps into these hopes.

Micah 5:2(1) serves as a source text in the Gospels to draw attention to the parallels between David and Jesus. Not only was Jesus a descendant of David, but like David, Jesus was also born in the small town of Bethlehem (see Matt 2:5–6). The wise men from the East and Herod are informed that the messiah’s birth in Bethlehem is foretold in Mic 5:2–3(1–2). While the New Testament writers treated the verse as a prognostication, modern scholars do not typically treat Mic 5:2 as a messianic prediction in its original context.41 Rather, Mic 5:2–3 refers to the hometown of David in the eleventh century BCE, three centuries before the eighth-century prophet Micah and likely another two to three centuries before this text was penned in the postexilic period. Specific dates for this text range from the sixth to the fourth centuries BCE.42 Micah 5:2 anticipates a new king from the Davidic line who will restore the kingdom of the sons of Israel as it was in the time of David and Solomon. Matthew and the other Gospel writers go to considerable lengths to make certain their readers see Jesus as a different kind of king, one who is not interested in political power.

3(2) Micah 5:3(2) requires the identification of several entities as well as a decision about how this verse relates to its context. The first question to answer is the identity of the he that is the subject of give. Does this he refer to Yahweh or to the ruler? Syntactically, this is not an easy question because both Yahweh and the ruler appear in the third person in the surrounding verses.43 Determining the identity of this third-person reference must rely upon how one interprets the action of the remainder of the verse. The idea of sending the people of Judah into exile before bringing them back makes sense in the context of divine judgment, whereas associating such action with the king lacks motivation. Yahweh must therefore be assumed as the one surrendering them up.

The third-person masculine plural reference to them refers formally back to the tribes of Judah, which also appears to be the same group called his brothers in 5:3b(2b), the group who will return to the sons of Israel.44 The third-person masculine singular pronoun attached to the word brothers assumes that the figure who comes from Bethlehem and the clans of Judah are related in some way. The identity implied by the phrase sons of Israel is, however, also not as clear to decipher as one might wish. Scholars often assume this group refers to the Judeans returning from the exile to their brothers in the land, or to a combination of the twelve tribes that comprised the united kingdom who were the sons of Jacob/Israel and who are frequently cited as the sons of Israel elsewhere in the Old Testament?45

The identities of the one … giving birth and the child have also been interpreted in various ways, including the child as a messianic figure, or as a reference to Lady Zion and the birth of her children. Several commentators see 5:3(2) as an allusion to Isa 7:14 in light of the reference to the woman giving birth (Mic 4:9–10) and the coming ruler (Mic 5:2[1]). This group tends to interpret the one giving birth as an announcement of a new Davidic ruler.46 The possibility of an allusion appears strong at first glance since the context in Isaiah contains several different parallels. The lexical parallels are striking and represent an unusual way to announce a birth.

Isaiah 7:14

Micah 5:3(2)



Therefore, the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and he shall name him Immanuel.

Therefore, he will give them up until the time that the one bearing a child has given birth, and the rest of his brothers will return to the sons of Israel.



The differences between the two passages are, however, significant. Isaiah 7:14 announces a sign, with the word “sign” serving as the direct object of “give.” The name of the son means “God is with us,” which suggests the child will be an omen of hope for divine protection. The verb give in Mic 5:3 has an attached pronominal suffix as direct object, but it uses the word ntn to mean “give up” or “turn over.” It announces punishment.

Others have treated the reference as a signal of imminence, that is, a metaphor for any woman having a child, meaning that the birth will happen within “the necessary interval” to prepare for restoration of the entire people.47 Still others suggest that the metaphor serves a dual function: (1) to infer that the pain of childbirth is the time of punishment (connecting to Mic 4:9) and (2) to anticipate the time of a future ruler (with reference to Isa 7:14 and 9:5–6).48

In the end, one must identify these entities in order to make sense of the verse in its context. Consequently, one must first decide the identity of the figure who gives up the tribes. Those who believe Mic 5:3(2) refers to the ruler, do so because the ruler is the subject of the verbs in 5:2(1), 4(3). They assume that 5:3(2) also contains a description of the actions of this ruler. By contrast, those who interpret this third-person reference as Yahweh also draw upon an understanding of form. Since 5:3(2) begins with therefore, the verse makes sense as a prophetic oracle that announces the decision of Yahweh to act. In this interpretation, Yahweh gives up the tribes of Judah (to their enemy) until the tribes will reunite and return to the land. As such, it represents a delayed promise that Yahweh will punish the tribes of Judah for a time, but the duration of that punishment will be limited because ultimately the ruler and the remainder of his brothers will return.

The phrase return to used here translates the Hebrew šûb + ʿal, but this phrase must be translated contextually since the combination of the verb with this preposition can mean “to turn upon” (Exod 14:26; 15:19), “to return against” (2 Sam 16:8), or “to return to” (Gen 40:13; 41:13; Num 33:7; Josh 19:12). The closest parallel would appear to be the last group where the combined preposition and verb is used to indicate the return destination point. The destination, however, is not expressed in purely geographical terms. The ruler and his brothers will return to the sons of Israel. This term has familial connotations and political implications since Israel (Jacob) fathered the ancestors of the twelve tribes that comprised the united kingdom; the promise suggests this new David will return and function as a ruler in Israel (5:2[1]). The territory will extend beyond Judah to include the territory of all the sons of Israel.

The question of the context of this delayed promise must also be considered. Modern scholars frequently interpret this verse, and its context, as an oracle whose author speaks to an exilic or postexilic audience to offer hope for restoration of the Davidic monarchy following the destruction of 587 BCE. Yet, to do so, scholars must assume that this verse functions as part of an anthology (usually portions of chs. 4–5) inserted into the middle of the book. Why would an editor place a preformulated promise of restoration of the Davidic monarchy into this context if this promise holds little hope of being actualized? One might see in 5:2–4(1–3) an oblique allusion to the hopes that certain parties had for the governorship of Zerubbabel, the grandson of Jehoiachin (the Davidic king taken from Jerusalem into exile in the first deportation of 597 BCE). Hope for Zerubbabel certainly plays a role in Haggai and Zech 1–8 in this respect (see esp. Hag 2:20–23; Zech 4:6–10). The promise in Amos 9:11–12 (also considered a hopeful addition to Amos from the exilic period) represents another particularly clear parallel to Mic 5:2–3 in that it articulates a hope for a reconstitution of the Davidic monarchy with a Judean king centered in Jerusalem:

11On that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen, and repair its breaches, and raise up its ruins, and rebuild it as in the days of old; 12in order that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name, says the LORD who does this. (NRSV)

The fallen booth of David likely refers to Jerusalem or to Judah, and the phrase “all the nations over whom my name is called” is interpreted as the boundaries of Israel at the time of David and Solomon, territory that also included control of Edom according to the accounts in 2 Sam 8:12, 14, as well as other surrounding peoples. As such, this promise inherently articulates a Judean vision of what a reunified kingdom would look like.

Nevertheless, such a reading creates real dilemmas for at least two reasons. First, and perhaps most importantly, it forces the reader to assume a perspective that is not clearly signaled in the text by forcing the reader to relocate the reading of this text so that it reflects issues of concern for the late exilic or early postexilic period. Second, the assumption that 5:1(2) alludes to the role of Zerubbabel ignores the fact that such allusion is quite oblique. In fact, both of these observations run counter to the context, an observation amplified by the fact that the second-person masculine singular addressees of this larger unit (mentioned in 4:8; 5:2[1]) frame three sayings that all begin with now and seem to expect that the reader of these verses interpret them in light of the action of the book associated with an eighth-century prophet. These observations become even more acute when one recognizes that the third group of sayings in chapters 4–5 is characterized by the recurring use of and it will be (wəhāyâ) that appears four times (5:5[4], 7[6], 8[7], 10[9]) at the beginning of the subunits and consequently points the reader to the future. At the same time, the enemy explicitly mentioned in 5:5(4) is Assyria, not Babylon (which one would expect if this section were intended to evoke the period of the exile). To be sure, Mic 4:10 mentions Babylon explicitly, so the expectation of an exilic context is not completely without contextual signal. Nevertheless, it will be necessary to return to this question after looking at 5:5(4).

4(3) Micah 5:4(3) returns to a description of the ruler’s character that guides his leadership and the consequences for the people. This characterization of the ruler’s kingship represents the ideals of the righteous king that are consistent with expectations of kings elsewhere in the Old Testament and the ancient Near East.49 The statement that he will stand has a performative aspect that should not be glossed over. It presents the king as one who accepts a role of authority (cf. Isa 3:3). The precise formulations of Mic 5:4 are, however, unique in Old Testament literature. The phrases “to shepherd in strength” or “to shepherd in the strength of Yahweh” do not appear elsewhere, but they draw upon the shepherd imagery portraying the king’s role as military commander leading the forces of Yahweh in the battle.50 This language is particularly at home in the Psalter where psalmists speak about Yahweh’s strength or address Yahweh directly about “your strength” on a regular basis.51

The verse also expects the royal figure to perform his role as shepherd in the pride of the name of Yahweh, a phrase that also appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. The word pride means splendor. It assumes a king who regulates his behavior by his religious commitment to Yahweh takes on qualities from Yahweh as well. In this sense, this portrayal comports with the view of kingship in Deut 17:14–20, although Mic 5:4 lacks a specific connection to the king reading the instruction (tôrâ) of Yahweh that appears so prominently in Deut 17:18–20. The phrase Yahweh his God is used in Samuel and Kings to describe the ideal relationship between the king and Yahweh, especially with reference to David, Solomon, and their descendants.52

The name of Yahweh raises several significant issues of theological significance. As noted previously, 5:2–4(1–3) subtly but consistently downplays the role of the kingly figure to stress Yahweh as the King. The same happens in 5:4 with the description of the royal figure. The text states that he will shepherd in the pride (i.e., splendor) of the name of Yahweh. This phrasing reflects a significant aspect of Deuteronomic and Deuteronomistic theology concerning the presence of Yahweh. The classic expression of this idea appears in Deut 12:5: “But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes as his habitation to put his name there” (NRSV). The phrase comes to be associated with the Jerusalem temple, but it plays a more prominent role once the temple is destroyed. As a theological concept, the image of the temple as a place where Yahweh chose to put his name distinguishes itself from temple concepts that assumed Yahweh’s glory (kābōd) was actually present in the temple because of the ark of the covenant.53 Conceptualizing the temple as the place where Yahweh chose to put his name gave more prominence to the conceptualization of Yahweh dwelling in the heavens. Yahweh chose to put his name at the temple in Jerusalem and there he was to be worshiped because Yahweh is present wherever Yahweh’s name appears. In Mic 5:4, the royal figure reflects a subordinate image. The royal figure gains no prestige as king. Rather, whatever he does reflects the presence of Yahweh through Yahweh’s name.

A significant number of commentators treat 5:4(3) as the original continuation of 5:2(1), arguing that the reference to the action of Yahweh in 5:3(2) interrupts the description of the ruler, and thus represents a secondary insertion.54 While this is true, that observation does not necessitate the assumption that 5:3 comes from a different hand. In fact, 8Ḥev 1 5:3b translates “they will return” as a promise that makes better sense if 5:4 assumes that someone has been forced to leave. Indeed, forced departure is precisely in view with the phrase he (i.e., Yahweh) will give them up in 5:3. The verb ntn can be used to mean surrender someone to someone else (e.g., Lam 3:20; Judg 6:13; 11:9; Deut 2:31; Ps 44:12). Apart from 5:3 one would have to go all the way back to 4:10 to find another text that could account for the dispersal of Yahweh’s people outside Yahweh’s land. It seems unwise, therefore, to remove 5:3 as a later insertion because 5:4b assumes the presence of 5:3.





C. AND IT WILL BE (5:5–9[4–8])


5And this will be peace.

Assyria, though he enters our land and though he treads on our citadels,a

we will raiseb against him seven shepherds and eight leadersc of men.

6And they will shepherd the landd of Assyria with a sword,

and the land of Nimrode with a dagger,f

and he will deliverg from Assyria though he enters our land,

and though he treads upon our border.

7And the remnanth of Jacob will be in the midst of many peoples, like dew from Yahweh,

like abundant showersi on the grass

which does not depend upon humanity,

and does not wait for the children of humans.

8And the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations,

in the midst of many peoples likej a lion in the high places of the forest,

like a (young)k lion among the flocks of sheep who, if he passes through,

will trample, and tear, and will not deliver.

9You will raise your hand against your adversaries,

and all your enemies will be cut off.

a. The LXX paraphrases this line and it differs considerably from the Greek in 8Ḥev 1. The LXX translates both instances of kî in MT with hotan, which implies an indefinite time but does not imply doubt that something will come about: hence, “at the time when.” The LXX has tēn chōran hēmōn (“our country”) while 8Ḥev 1 appears to translate tas bar[eis hēmōn] (“our citadels”), though an important part of the text is missing. The LXX and 8Ḥev 1 use two slightly different sets of verbs. The first pair (epelthē and elthē respectively) translate the Hebrew root bōʾ. The meaning of epelthē in the LXX can connote negative movement, “to attack,” while elthē in 8Ḥev 1 has a more generic sense of “going,” though if 8Ḥev 1 does attest “citadels,” then “entering our citadels” would also signify an attack. The LXX does not include the second Hebrew clause (yidrôk bəʾarməʾnôtênû, meaning “he will tread upon our citadels”) in its paraphrase.

b. The LXX understands the first-person common plural Hebrew verb wahəqêmônû (“we shall raise up”) as a third-person plural verb epegerthēsontai (“they shall be raised up”), making “seven shepherds” into the subject rather than the object of the verb as in the Hebrew. The Hebrew form in MT could be read as third-person plural in the unpointed Hebrew of MT (which would only have had the consonants whqmnw). The Greek manuscript, 8Ḥev 1, has epegeroumen (which here probably connotes “we rise up”). It thus also translates the Hebrew root qûm with a synonymous verb root, but reads the Hebrew consonants as first-person plural like the pointed text of MT. These are simply variant readings of the unpointed text.

c. The LXX translates nəsîkê (“leaders,” from nəsîkê II) with dēgmata (“bites,” “attacks”). In so doing, it perhaps chose a different Hebrew word that is nearly a homonym when retroverted back into unpointed Hebrew. The LXX translator read nšyky while the MT consonants reflect nsyky (see Gen 49:17; Jer 8:17; Amos 9:3). Because nəsîkê II (“leaders”) is parallel to “shepherds,” it makes more sense to follow MT. The change was likely deliberate. The LXX translator may have sought to avoid MT (nəsîkê II) because nəsîkê I can refer to a molten image that is cast from metal.

d. The word “land” is not present in the LXX, but it is present in the Greek manuscript from Nahal Hever (8Ḥev 1), thus confirming MT.

e. The Hebrew place-name Nimrod appears four times in the Old Testament (Gen 10:8, 9; 1 Chr 1:10; Mic 5:6) and once in Jubilees (8:7), where it is always translated as Nebrōd in Greek.

f. MT reads “with its entrances” (biptāḥêhā), likely due to accidental transposition. The assumption here of bappətîḥâ (with a dagger) involves the early transposition of two letters in the unpointed Hebrew text. The MT has bptḥyh (which literally means, “in her opening”) while the original bptyḥh offers a clear parallel to sword in the previous clause, though it is a much less common word, appearing elsewhere only in Ps 55:22. The LXX has a dative form of taphros (which means “trench”), and probably assumes the consonants of MT, so the loss of “dagger” would have been an early scribal error.

g. MT lacks a direct object on the verb wəhiṩîl (“and he will deliver”). BHS proposes adding the first-person common plural suffix to provide the expected suffix (whṩylnw), but without citing textual affirmation in ancient versions. The LXX and 8Ḥev 1 both agree with MT and with one another (rusetai, with no object). The sentence is awkward, but there is no evidence to support adding the suffix.

h. The LXX and 8Ḥev 1 use different Greek words for “remnant” in the phrase “the remnant of Jacob” in Mic 5:7[6; 7 LXX]. The former uses to hypolemma tou Iakōb while 8Ḥev 1 does not have the articles and translates the phrase as kataloipon Iakōb. Hence, despite the differences in Greek words, both texts reflect the Hebrew of MT.

i. The Hebrew word rəbîbîm (translated here abundant showers) appears only six times in the Old Testament, so it is relatively rare (Deut 32:2; Pss 65:11; 72:6; Jer 3:3; 14:22; Mic 5:7[6]). Its meaning was apparently not well known either since each translator went a different direction with the Greek translation of the Hebrew. They all seem to be attempting to reason out what word should really be translated. Deuteronomy 32:2 translates it as niphetos, which means “snow,” which would be šeleg in Hebrew. The two texts from Psalms (65:11; 72:6) both use plural forms of the Greek word stargōn, which means “droplets” and would presume a plural form of the Hebrew word deleph. The translators of Psalms and Deuteronomy thus intuit that the word has something to do with water from the sky. The translator of Jeremiah uses a different Greek word in 3:3 than in 14:22. In Jer 3:3, the translator opts for a plural noun, poimenas, which means “shepherds” and reflects the Hebrew word roʿîm, while in Jer 14:22 the translator uses a singular form of the noun plēsmonē, which reflects one of the noun forms of the Hebrew root śbʿ, since the word plēsmonē means “satiation.” Here in Mic 5:7, the translator chooses the Greek word arnes, a plural noun meaning “lambs.” This word presumes the Hebrew kešeb. While some of these translations attempt to find better-known Hebrew words that sound similar to the MT rəbîbîm, others try to reason something that makes sense from the context. In all probability, the scarcity of the word caused considerable difficulty for the various translators, but this does not mean that the MT should be changed.

j. The MT and Mur 88 have different prepositions on the front of the Hebrew word for young lion. MT has a k while Mur 88 has a b. These two letters are easily confused, and both can make a certain sense, but the b on Mur 88 sounds more awkward in English: “The remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, with a lion in the high places of the forest” (Mur 88). The k preposition in the MT makes the relevant phrase into a simile: The remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion in the high places of the forest (MT).

k. The MT has two words for lion in 5:8(7). The LXX translates the second word for lion in the MT with skymnos rather than leōn. The Greek word skymnos means “cub,” meaning that the LXX translator understood the Hebrew word kəfîr to refer to a lion cub or a young lion, though most English lexica assume or state that a kəfîr was old enough to hunt on its own prey while the word gûr II is recognized as a word for a cub that is not yet weaned (see esp. Lam 4:3, as well as Gen 49:9; Deut 33:22; Ezek 19:2–3, 5; Nah 2:12).

Though notoriously difficult to translate, Mic 5:5(4) nevertheless plays an important role as the opening verse of the third group of sayings in Mic 4–5 that all begin with the phrase and it will be, a phrase that represents a single word in Hebrew (wəhāyâ). In addition to 5:5(4), this introductory marker puts the action in the future and appears in 5:7(6), 8(7), 10(9). Together, the four occurrences of wəhāyâ (and it will be) characterize the third group of sayings identified in Mic 4–5. Syntactically, the first and last of these introductions create problems that likely arose from an editorial decision to add wəhāyâ statements in 5:5(4) and 5:10(9) when this preexisting unit was incorporated into its current context.55

5(4) In order to understand 5:5(4), several observations are in order. First, the MT has divided the verse unevenly and has placed the strong disjunctive atnach on only the third word (peace), meaning that 5:5a(4a) has only three words (wəhāyâ zeh šālôm) while the second half of the verse begins with the word Assyria. Nevertheless, most English translations seek ways to include Assyria with the word peace, either by assuming peace should be pointed as a construct form and translated “peace of Assyria” or by assuming the presence of a preposition that is not explicitly present when translating “peace with Assyria.” Certainly, both explanations could account for the unpointed Hebrew text without emendation. Yet, following this line of interpretation requires questioning why the MT does not combine these two words. The translation used here attempts, instead, to do justice to the MT by keeping 5:5a(4a) syntactically separate from 5:5b(4b). Second, unless one interprets the pronoun (zeh) proleptically as an introduction to what follows (“And this will be peace”), the masculine singular pronoun must refer to the ruler who is the subject of 5:2–4(1–3). Such a view is arguably the most natural syntactical interpretation of the pronoun zeh, but it expresses a very cumbersome thought that equates a person with peace: “And this one will be peace.” Third, assuming that the pronoun refers back to the ruler creates a strange dynamic in which 5:5a(4a) both essentially ends the statements about the ruler who was the subject of 5:2–4(1–3) and represents the conclusion of the second group of sayings that share the same beginning sound. It must be noted that 5:5(4) begins with wəhāyâ (“and it will be”), which characterizes the third group of sayings that all begin with this word (5:5[4], 7[6], 8[7], 10[9]). This verbal form is then followed by the pronoun zeh which serves as the subject. In this sense, 5:5a(4a) serves a transitional function that probably stems from the compiler who joined the sayings of chapters 4–5 together: it summarizes 5:2–4(1–3), but it begins like 5:7(6), 8(7), 10(9).56 The fact that a very similar linkage appears in the transition between this third group that begins with wəhāyâ and the fourth group of sayings that are characterized by the repetition of I will cut off (5:10aβ[9aβ], 11[10], 12[11], 13[12]) further suggests that the links between these groups have been facilitated by the compiler who brought them together in the context of Mic 4–5.57

The second half of 5:5(4) abruptly changes the topic from the ruler of Judah to Assyria, as evident from the Masoretic pointing of the verse, which makes Assyria stand alone at the beginning of 5:5b(4b) before the onset of the conditional clause that follows. This clause states a condition, formulated as a threat from Assyria (though he enters our land and though he treads upon our citadels) that the informed reader knows will happen. This condition, however, is undercut by the following affirmation: we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men. This numerical saying can be interpreted in one of two ways. The use of numerical chains can be interpreted as an indefinite number, a more figurative means of saying “several” (so, e.g., the refrain in Amos’s oracles against the nations “for three transgressions and for four”: Amos 1:3, 6, 9, 11, 13; 2:1, 4, 6; see also Jer 36:23; Eccl 11:2). Scholars typically interpret the numerical chain in Mic 5:4 in this figurative fashion, but a second way in which biblical writers utilize numerical chains merits further consideration. Specifically, there are places where two numbers are used to relate several things where the second number actually coincides with the number of elements listed in the saying. For example, consider Prov 30:15–16:

Three things are never satisfied; four never say, “Enough”:

Sheol, the barren womb, the earth ever thirsty for water,

and the fire that never says, “Enough.” (NRSV)

Additionally, Prov 30:18–19 uses the same “three … four” pattern, and lists four things:

Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand:

the way of an eagle in the sky,

the way of a snake on a rock,

the way of a ship on the high seas,

and the way of a man with a girl. (NRSV)

Other examples also follow this pattern, and the fact that they appear in Proverbs suggests the possibility that this formulaic speech could have played a role in educational contexts within wisdom circles.58 This second avenue of interpretation actually holds considerable appeal in Mic 5:5(4). Interpreted in this manner, the numerical statement in 5:5(4) (we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men against him) would recognize the parallel terms, shepherds and leaders, as synonyms, meaning that 5:5(4) should be read as a pronouncement that eight kings will shepherd the people. Read as a prediction of what will happen from the time of Hezekiah’s reign (cf. Mic 1:1) when Assyria laid siege to Jerusalem, eight kings ruled Judah before the temple and the city were destroyed in 587 BCE: Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah. The consequence of this reading takes on greater significance in the verse that follows.

6(5) Micah 5:6(5) builds upon the announcement in 5:5(4) that we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight leaders of men. Whereas 5:5(4) announced they are coming, 5:6(5) describes what they will do. This description evokes vocabulary from the preceding verse, creating a cohesively formulated saying that communicates both the threat of Assyrian incursion and the role of the shepherds repelling that threat.

5:5(4) Though he enters our land,

We will raise shepherds.

5:6(5) They will shepherd,

Though he enters our land.

The parallelism of these two verses is significant because the formulation of the task that the shepherds perform deviates significantly from the typical actions of shepherds that one finds elsewhere when the verb shepherd appears with the direct object.59 The key to understanding 5:6(5), however, lies in the weapons held by the shepherd. Rather than the staff, which can be used to guide and defend the flock, the shepherd in 5:6(5) utilizes a sword and a dagger. Consequently, 5:6(5) depicts hostile action of the shepherd directed against the land of Assyria. Here, the close association of 5:6(5) with 5:5(4) confirms this hostility since 5:6b(5b) reminds the reader that Assyria will enter our land using the same phrase as 5:5a(4a) to refer to Assyrian incursion. Additionally, 5:6b(5b) assumes the shepherds’ action results in deliverance. Equally important in this scenario is the parallel term land of Nimrod in 5:6b(5b). The use of Nimrod to parallel Assyria implies the broader Mesopotamian region in general. The Table of Nations in Gen 10:8–11 describes Nimrod as the son of Cush whose kingdom began with Babylon before he created Nineveh. By depicting the object of the sword and the dagger as the land of Assyria and the land of Nimrod, Mic 5:6(5) extends the threat of foreign incursion beyond the time of Assyrian hegemony to evoke the threat of Babylon as well. Hence, 5:5–6(4–5) takes a long view of the role of Judah’s shepherds fending off Assyria (and Babylon), even while recognizing Assyria will invade the land. This portrait comports well with the portrait of Judah’s history from the time of Hezekiah until the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE.60 The threat from Assyria will become a sign of deliverance in 5:6(5), but that does not mean Judah will escape unscathed. Consequently, the promise of deliverance gives way to a new subject in 5:7(6), 8(7): the remnant of Jacob.

7–8(6–7) The next two verses (5:7–8[6–7]) constitute a thematic pairing that focuses upon the remnant of Jacob. Each verse begins with the characteristic verb—and it will be (wəhāyâ)—that unites this third group of sayings (5:5–9[4–8]), and the phrase remnant of Jacob immediately follows this introductory marker in 5:7(6), 8(7). The term remnant should be treated as a polyvalent word. On the one hand, it connotes a promise that implies some will survive. On the other hand, the term implies some will die. Moreover, both verses that begin with the phrase and the remnant of Jacob will be continue with statements that force the reader to consider the statements in relationship to one another through repetition:

7(6): And the remnant of Jacob will be in the midst of many peoples.

8(7): And the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples.

Both verses depict the future remnant of Jacob living outside the land and stress that the remnant is widely scattered. This language thus refers to diaspora populations, but the term remnant of Jacob also draws them together as part of the family. Jacob was the father of twelve sons, each of whom were allotted a portion of the land (Josh 13–23). By naming these displaced populations the remnant of Jacob these verses convey the idea these communities are still related to those in the land. It also expands the promise to those who were scattered by Assyria and Babylon, to those exiled from Israel as well as Judah.

Yet, the two verses also use different metaphors to highlight two distinct aspects of the future remnant. Micah 5:7(6) depicts the numerical fertility of the remnant by comparing the remnant to the abundant dew that feeds the grass, while 5:8(7) focuses upon the terrifying power of the remnant using the metaphor of a lion capable of terrorizing the sheep. Micah 5:7(6) describes a healthy, fertile people using images of vitality: the dew/showers from Yahweh that do not depend upon human actions. Micah 5:8(7) portrays the future remnant of Zion as a fearsome lion that travels where it will and can attack violently if it so chooses. These perspectives focus upon the future and upon the promissory elements of the remnant of Jacob, who will be numerous and powerful.

9(8) The concluding threat that the lion poses in 5:8(7) provides the impetus for 5:9(8) as it transitions to the fourth and final group of sayings in chapters 4–5. Micah 5:9(8) reads like a transitional verse between the third and fourth group. Like other transitional verses (see 4:8; 5:2[1]) in this compilation, 5:9(8) returns to the second-person masculine singular address. The identity of the second-person masculine singular addressee is not, however, easy to discern. Read with 5:8(7), the you in 5:9(8) articulates a scenario in which the nation (like the lion) will act against its enemies.61 In so doing, the niphal third-person masculine plural verb yikkārētû becomes the last word of the last phrase of 5:9(8), but it also anticipates the recurring Leitwort for the concluding unit (5:10–15[9–14]) where the hiphil perfect first-person common singular form of the same verb (hikrattî) appears in 5:10–13(9–12) to explicate Yahweh’s removal of the enemies. Consequently, since 5:9(8) anticipates 5:10–15(9–14), where Yahweh is clearly the speaker who announces I will cut off, one can also interpret 5:9(8) as a prayer to Yahweh affirming that Yahweh will remove the enemies from the land. This ambiguity is very much in keeping with the transitional function of the verse.

The content of 5:9(8) consists of two poetic versets using parallelismus memborum in an ABBA pattern. Two verbal expressions (raise your hand, be cut off) form the outer elements of the frame while two synonyms for your antagonists (adversaries, enemies) constitute the internal word pairs. Further, the semantic interplay between the two versets reflects a simple cause and effect relationship. The expression “to raise one’s hand against” implies a physical attack in the first half while the second half of the line expresses the consequence that the enemies will be annihilated.





D. ON THAT DAY I WILL CUT OFF (5:10–15[9–14])


10And it will be on that day, utterance of Yahweh, that I will cut off your horses from your midst,

and I will cause your chariots to perish.a

11And I will cut off the cities of your land,

and I will throw downb your fortifications.

12And I will cut off c sorcery from your hand,

and you will no longer have soothsayers.

13And I will cut off your images and your pillars from your midst,

and you will no longer bow down to the work of your hands.

14And I will pull up your Asherimd from your midst,

and I will destroy your cities.

15And in anger and rage, I will execute vengeance on the nations who did not listen.

a. The LXX translates as apolō, which comes from the Greek word apollumi, forms of which routinely appear in the LXX with only one lambda. Typically, the word means destroy, which makes it a suitable translation for the hiphil forms of ʾbd.

b. The LXX uses exarō here to translate the qal form of the root hrs, but uses the exact word (exarō) to translate the hiphil form of krt in the next verse. The double use of exarō does not point to a different Hebrew text, but to the likelihood that the translator could not think of another synonym for “destroy.” Also, the word exariō appears in several other biblical passages to translate a hiphil first-person common singular form of krt (e.g., 1 Sam 20:15 [twice]; Zeph 1:3, 4; Ezek 14:8, 13, 17).

c. See the previous note.

d. The Septuagint routinely translates Asherah/Asherim with the Greek word alsos which means “grove” or “sacred grove.” The latter refers to groves of trees where cultic activities took place. In this sense, the translation comes close to those passages in the Old Testament that seem to assume that an Asherah was a carved wooden pole used in a worship setting and castigated as an idol. See, for example, 1 Kgs 15:13; 2 Kgs 21:7; 23:4, 6; 2 Chr 15:16.

10(9) The fourth and final group of sayings (5:10–15[9–14]) begins with a series of formulaic elements. Micah 5:10(9) overloads the introductory clauses with the formulas of the previous group, and it will be (wəhāyâ) and the eschatological day sayings that began the first group in chapter 4 (on that day, cf. 4:6), followed by the hiphil perfect first-person common singular form (wəhikrattî) that leads off the next three verses and holds the unit together by reiterating its theme. The overloaded introduction suggests that the elements comprising 5:10aα(9aα) were deliberately constructed for the context to introduce the following verses. The opening of 5:10aβ(9aβ) bears the consistent style of the unit since and I will cut off begins each verse from 5:10ab(9ab) through 5:13(12). The content of this unit sets these verses apart from the immediately preceding material, even though 5:9(8) also ended with the verb cut off. These distinctions suggest that 5:10aβ–13(9aβ–12) existed independently, and that it was adapted to fit the context. These distinctions from the preceding include the change of speaker, the nature of the offense, and the identity of the enemies. While 5:9(8) addressed Yahweh, Yahweh is clearly the speaker in 5:10–15(9–14). The nature of the actions implies the kind of power typically associated with Yahweh, not a human: removal of the ability to make war, destruction of the cities, removal of sorcery, destruction of idols, and execution of vengeance. These elements suggest that 5:10aβ–13(9aβ–12) originally served as a pronouncement against Yahweh’s own people, while the editor who brought this composition into its current location has done so with the purpose of condemning foreign nations who will act against Judah.62

Following the introduction, 5:10(9) announces the destruction of the power to wage war with the elimination of the horses and chariots. These elements constitute military weaponry, not a typical means of locomotion.

11(10) Micah 5:11(10) continues logically from 5:10(9). Without the ability to attack using horses and chariots, the cities will be vulnerable. The two halves of this verse pronounce Yahweh’s devastation upon the cities and fortifications. The word fortifications refers to the physical defenses erected in key cities that enable the city to withstand attacks. Without such fortifications, which Yahweh will throw down, no city would be able to withstand an enemy attack.

12(11) With 5:12(11), the focus turns from military threats to the condemnation of religious practices through 5:14(13). The word sorcery appears only twelve times in the Old Testament.63 The word carries a polemical connotation, as is evident by the fact that these references either appear in lists of inappropriate behavior or are associated with the religious practice of Assyria (Nah 3:4) or Babylon (Isa 47:9, 12; Jer 27:9; Dan 2:2).64 One may infer from several of these texts that the practice of sorcery was associated with the worship of foreign deities and that the practice of sorcery represents sinful behavior on the part of those who are attempting to imitate (largely) Mesopotamian practices.65 The word translated here as soothsayers is actually a participial form from the denominative verb ʿnn, which derives from the noun “cloud.” The divinatory practice may have originally implied interpreting omens in the clouds.66 It seems to refer generally to those interpreting signs in natural phenomena.67

13(12) This verse condemns the worship of idols. As with 5:12(11), these terms appear in polemical contexts, and are frequently associated with practices adopted in Israel as a result of mixing with the nations.68 In Isa 10:5–12, Israel and Judah are both condemned for their adoption of practices associated with the worship of idols (10:11) and this is the reason Yahweh decides to send Assyria to punish Samaria and Jerusalem even though he knows it will require him to punish Assyria as well (10:12). The pillars refer to stone monuments that represent other deities.69

14(13) The Asherim mentioned in 5:14(13) can refer to different things depending upon the context.70 It can refer to a deity, and it can refer to the tree symbol in iconographic portrayals of that deity. Asherah has also been interpreted as the ancient consort of Yahweh in some contexts.71 In 5:14(13), the plural form eliminates a direct reference to the deity. Instead, your Asherim may refer to poles used to represent the tree of life that serve as the focal point of worship condemned by the worshipers of Yahweh only.72

As evident from the background of those things condemned in 5:12–14(11–13), the condemnation of certain practices generally signals that the very same practices have found their way into the worship of Israel and Judah. Consequently, and not surprisingly, quite a number of scholars have suggested that the core of this unit originally pronounced judgment against Yahweh’s own people, but these sayings were reformulated in the editorial frame of 5:9–10(8–9), 15(14) as judgments against the nations who will attack Judah.73 In their final form, the compiler of chapters 4–5 included these pronouncements as punishment of the worship of idols for the nations. This idea represents a significant theological development in postexilic Judah.

15(14) The concluding verse of chapters 4–5 offers a final comment upon the preceding verses, in the process interpreting 5:9(8), 10–14(9–13) as the pronouncements of judgment upon the nations who will attack Judah in the future. Micah 5:15(14) defines the judgment against the enemies as divine judgment by claiming that the nations who did not listen provoked Yahweh’s anger. While most of 5:10–15(9–14) reads like an announcement of judgment against Judah because of its syncretistic practices, the framing verses (5:9[8], 10[9], 15[14]) clearly interpret the action as directed against the nations. The pronouncement of the punishment of the nations hostile to Yahweh appears at first glance to run counter to the message of the opening unit of this larger block since 4:1–7 opened with a much more positive message toward the nations in which war ceased (4:3) because the nations submitted themselves to Yahweh’s reign. Yet, the two units are not as incompatible as they seem at first glance.

The four groups of texts that comprise Mic 4–5 (4:1–7; 4:8–5:4[3]; 5:5–9[4–8]; 5:10–15[9–14]) intertwine lexically, but they also focus upon four recurring themes as they portray the future: the changing role of the nations, the fate of Zion, the reaffirmation of Davidic leadership, and the nature of the remnant community. The opening unit (4:1–7) describes life in the distant future (the end of days in Mic 4:1), while the remaining groups back up and explore the journey of how Jerusalem and the nations will get there. The first group of sayings (4:1–7) lays out the end game: peace for Zion and the remnant in the last days because the nations recognize Yahweh as king and seek his instruction in Jerusalem. The second group (4:8–5:4[3]) changes the chronological focus to that of the current generation that is threatened in the time of Hezekiah to refer to the time of the prophet based upon 1:1 (e.g., the use of now in 4:9, 10, 11, 14). While this second group still promises ultimate restoration to Zion (4:8), it also anticipates distress for Zion (4:9–10) and Zion’s king (4:14), exile to Babylon (4:10), and attacks from foreign nations (4:11) before Yahweh’s plan to punish those nations also comes to fruition (4:12–13) and the continuance of the Davidic line will prevent complete destruction (5:2–4[1–3]). The third group (5:5–9[4–8]) promises peace in the coming time (and it will be), a peace that will outlast the Assyrian threat, even though only a remnant of Judah will survive. This third group thus both intensifies the problems that Judah must endure by anticipating a lengthy struggle against Assyria (5:5–6[4–5]) and affirms that a remnant will begin to flourish among the nations (5:7–8[6–7]). The fourth group (5:10–15[9–14]) culminates in a promise to cut off the nations who have not yet learned to listen to Yahweh (5:15[14]). While this section focuses upon the punishment of the hostile nations, it also describes a scenario that in many ways returns to the description that began chapter 4: The ability of the nations to wage war will be cut off (5:10[9]), and these nations will be punished with the loss of cities (5:11[10]). The punishment also includes the elimination of sorcery and idolatry (5:12–14[11–13]), thus preparing the ground for the nations’ ability to recognize Yahweh as king, or face retribution from Yahweh himself.

EXCURSUS: THE NATURE OF MICAH 4–5 AS COMPILATION

Micah 4–5 combines independent units that explore diverse themes, yet the arrangement of the units demonstrates signs of deliberate editorial cohesion within the smaller sayings and larger groups of material that have been brought together in this location. Given the nature of chapters 4–5, how does one read and interpret this material? The key, as has been noted, lies in the frequent vacillation of the chronological markers and the assumption of a reading perspective at the end of the eighth century BCE, the time of the prophet for whom the book is named. While not disputing the scholarly consensus that the compilation of the chapters as well as the dates of composition for the units that comprise chapters 4–5 takes place in the postexilic period, simply dating the oracles and their collection obscures the fact that the collection asks the reader, through clear textual signals, to project the message into the future (4:1, 6; 5:5–9[4–8], 10[9]), as well as to relate the events to now (4:9, 10, 11; 5:1 [4:14]). In so doing, the chapters take on an interpretive theological function: to provide both explanations for Jerusalem’s “coming” destruction and for the purposeful reconstitution of life with Yahweh as a remnant community that has endured its punishment.

Recently, scholars like Odil Steck, Karl van der Toorn, and David Carr have suggested ways that the scribal culture of Judah both shaped and was shaped by an educational system that produced and transmitted its own curriculum in the postexilic period.74 While the models of van der Toorn and Carr focus more on the scribal culture itself, Steck argues that the art of reading prophetic books in these scribal contexts needs to account for the book’s signals and the prophetic voice as the conveyor of that message.75 One can readily imagine that the compilation of Mic 4–5 arose in such a context. In Mic 4–5, the intertwining of motifs, the location of these chapters at the exact middle of the Book of the Twelve, and the way that these chapters interpret the epoch from Hezekiah forward suggest that their compilation played a key role in the developing sense of the importance of prophetic literature for teaching the ways of Yahweh over the span of history that ran from the eighth century BCE to the Persian period. For ruminations on the relative and absolute chronology of these chapters, see the introduction to Micah in this commentary.

Sweeney sees the two passages as introducing a debate regarding the role of the nations in the Persian period. 31. It is not uncommon in the ancient Near East for goddesses to be portrayed as warrior deities, either in their own quests or in support of the ruling king. These portrayals can also depict the goddess with zoomorphic imagery, both in texts and iconography. E.g., the Sumerian goddess Inana is compared to both a lion and a bull in her ability to destroy in an early text: “In heaven and on earth you roar like a lion and devastate the people. Like a huge wild bull you triumph over lands which are hostile. Like a fearsome lion you pacify the insubordinate and unsubmissive with your gall” (“Inana and Ebiḫ,” lines 7–9; cited from ETCSL [The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature]; http://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/]). Among other things, the goddess Ishtar was the goddess of war and is depicted carrying weapons in various iconographic exemplars. For example, see the seal depicting Ishtar with a bow and arrows in Jeremy Black and Anthony Green, “Ishtar,” in Dictionary of the Ancient Near East, ed. Piotr Bienkowski and Alan Millard (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2000), 156. Anat is depicted holding a shield, a spear, and a battle-axe. Sa-Moon Kang, Divine War in the Old Testament and in the Ancient Near East, BZAW 177 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1989), 78. The Sun Goddess of Arinna was also depicted as a powerful warrior (Kang, Divine War, 55). In these contexts, one also finds parallels where a goddess is depicted as a bull rather than a cow. Izak Cornelius, The Many Faces of the Goddess: The Iconography of the Syro-Palestinian Goddesses Anat, Astarte, Qedeshet, and Asherah c. 1500–1000 BCE, OBO 204 (Fribourg: Academic Press; Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2004), 30; and Buffie Johnson, Lady of the Beasts: Ancient Images of the Goddess and Her Sacred Animals (San Francisco: Harper & Row, 1988), 272.

32. See text note in the translation. The noun form of this root can refer generally to a band of people who are operating as raiding parties as in 1 Sam 30:8, 15, 23; 2 Sam 3:22; 2 Kgs 6:23; 13:20–21; Jer 18:22; Hos 7:1, etc. It can, however, also refer specifically to a group of warriors (e.g., Job 29:25; 2 Chr 25:9, 10, 13), including divine armies (Job 19:12; 25:3).

33. Wolff (142–43) adamantly declares that the phrase refers to the king of Judah, and specifically, King Zedekiah, who attempted to flee the Babylonians in 587 BCE. Mays (114) adds the additional note that the word “siege” is used against Jerusalem only with respect to Nebuchadnezzar’s siege against Jerusalem in 2 Kgs 24:10; 25:2; Jer 52:5; Ezek 4:3, 7; 5:2.

34. The phrase retains some level of ambiguity since Ps 3:7 could be an exception. There, the “wicked” represent the recipient of the blow, and it is combined with “knocking out the teeth” in the second (i.e., parallel) line of the verse.

35. E.g., Allen, 340. Andersen and Freedman describe the difficulties in detail, but do not take a clear stand (458–61). They see the reference to the striking of the judge in line with the defeat of the king in 4:9, but then point out that “there is no record of a king of Judah suffering such a fate in the time of Micah, so no identification is possible” (461). Smith-Christopher (163–65) argues for a composite text whose original meaning would have expressed the prophet’s lack of confidence in the Davidic line and his belief that the Assyrians would soon replace Hezekiah.

36. E.g., Mays, 114; Jeremias, 118–19. Wagenaar and Jeremias believe that the passage has been altered in the Seleucid period into something even larger, at least with the inclusion of 5:4b–5. Jan A. Wagenaar, Judgement and Salvation: The Composition and Redaction of Micah 2–5, VTSup 85 (Leiden: Brill, 2001), 278–89; and Jeremias, 187. Others see the verse as a reference to the siege of Sennacherib in 701 BCE, e.g., Allen, 341. Sweeney (2:376) acknowledges the late date of Mic 4–5, but treats the text synchronically, implying that it refers to the events of 701. De Jong explores how prophetic books were created as scribal reimaginings. Matthijs J. de Jong, “Biblical Prophecy—A Scribal Enterprise: The Old Testament Prophecy of Unconditional Judgement Considered as a Literary Phenomenon,” VT 61 (2011): 39–70, DOI: 10.1163/156853311X551493. De Jong treats Micah as a prime example of how an “earlier prophetic message … reflects the circumstances that occurred after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE” (63).

37. Several have noted that Egyptian tradition recorded by the fifth-century BCE historian Herodotus also contains a miracle account regarding the defeat of Sennacherib relating to the same military campaign as that described in 2 Kgs 19:35–37. The Egyptian miracle account speaks of the king Sethos who consulted the deity Vulcan and consequently led an untrained army against Sennacherib. On the night before the battle, mice purportedly managed to chew all the leather bowstring and shield handles of the Assyrian army so that they suffered heavy losses and fled from the Egyptians. See The History of Herodotus Parallel English/Greek English Translation, ed. and trans. G. C. Macaulay (London: Macmillan, 1890), 2:141.

38. See the discussion of the four groups of text structuring chs. 4–5 at the beginning of 4:1.

39. So Wolff, 144; Jeremias, 186. Wolff claims that the prophet is turning away from a Jerusalem-centered kingdom.

40. So Allen, 343.

41. Concerning the proclivities of the New Testament writers to adapt Old Testament texts for different theological purposes, see Dale C. Allison, The Intertextual Jesus: Scripture in Q (Harrisburg, PA: Trinity Press International, 2000), 1–24; Steve Moyise, “Intertextuality and the Study of the Old Testament in the New Testament,” in The Old Testament in the New Testament: Essays in Honour of J. L. North, ed. Steve Moyise, JSNTSup 189 (Sheffield: Sheffield Academic, 2000), 14–41. For specific and diverse interpretations of the reuse of Mic 5:1–2 in Matt. 2:5–6, see Maarten J. J. Menken, Matthew’s Bible: The Old Testament Text of the Evangelist, BETL 173 (Leuven: Leuven University Press, 2004), 257–62; Ulrich Luz, Matthew 1–7: A Commentary, CC (Minneapolis: Augsburg, 1985), 136; Robert F. Shedinger, “The Gospels and the Text of the Hebrew Bible: Micah 5:1 (Matt. 2:6) in Tatian’s Diatessaron,” in From Prophecy to Testament: The Function of the Old Testament in the New, ed. Craig A. Evans (Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 2004), 114–25, esp. 118–19; Allison, Intertextual Jesus, 196; G. K. Beale, Handbook on the New Testament Use of the Old Testament: Exegesis and Interpretation (Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2012), 56.

42. While some still maintain that the text could be preexilic, most mainstream scholarship since Stade at the end of the nineteenth century has treated this text as postexilic. For further discussion of these issues, see the introduction in this commentary.

43. Yahweh is mentioned in the third person in 4:13 and in 5:4(3). The ruler is referred to in the third person in 5:2(1), and in the second half of 5:3(2). The antecedent is complicated as well by the fact that 4:13 only refers to Yahweh in the third person, but the speaker there uses the first person as well. Contrast the interpretations of Sweeney (2:388) who states categorically that the he must be David and Mays (116) who just as certainly assumes that Yahweh must be the antecedent.

44. Contra Wolff (145) and others who interpret his brothers as a reference to those in the royal household.

45. The phrase sons of Israel appears over five hundred times in the Pentateuch and the Deuteronomistic History, usually in reference to the whole people of Israel, but the phrase can also be used to refer specifically to the people of the Northern Kingdom (e.g., 2 Kgs 17:7–9, 22, 24).

46. See Mays, 112–13; Wolff, 145; Jeremias, 184. By contrast, other commentators see the continuation of 4:9–10, and thus as referring to Lady Zion as the one giving birth, and the child as a representative of her inhabitants. So, Theodor Lescow, “Das Geburtsmotiv in den messianischen Weissagungen bei Jesaja und Micha,” ZAW 79 (1967): 204–5, DOI: 10.1515/zatw.1967.79.2.172; Rainer Kessler, Micha, HThKAT (Freiburg im Breisgau: Herder, 1999), 225–26. Rudolph (97) categorically denies this interpretation, but he offers no counter to Lescow beyond the mere assertion that it cannot refer to the eschatological end of the current crisis.

47. Sweeney, 2:388–89. Jeremias (184) offers similar logic, though he rejects the association of the one giving birth to Lady Zion. His rationale is not compelling. He rejects the arguments of Lescow and Kessler because the parallel texts they cite all use the comparative preposition “like.” Given the nature of poetic expression, this formal rationale seems forced.

48. Utzschneider, 113.

49. Kings in the ancient Near East served as warriors, judges, and priests because their roles involved the maintenance of law and order, protection (and/or expansion) of the territorial borders, and collecting taxes to help maintain a permanent military to enforce laws and protect boundaries. See Keith W. Whitelam, “King and Kingship,” ABD 4:40–48.

50. See the use of shepherd in military contexts, e.g., 1 Kgs 22:17 (= 2 Chr 18:16); Jer 6:3; 12:10.

51. Pss 21:2, 14; 28:7–8; 29:11; 46:2; 59:17–18; 62:8, 12; 63:3; 66:3; 68:29; 74:13; 77:15; 78:26, 61; 86:16; 89:11, 18; 93:1; 105:4; 118:14; 132:8; 140:8; 150:1.

52. See esp. 1 Sam 30:6; 1 Kgs 5:3; 11:4; 15:3–4.

53. Walther Zimmerli, Old Testament Theology in Outline (Edinburgh: T & T Clark, 1978), 77–79; Horst Dietrich Preuss, Old Testament Theology, trans. Leo G. Perdue, 2 vols., OTL (Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 1995), 1:170–71. See also Preuss’s discussion of “The Glory of Yahweh,” 1:167–70.

54. Jeremias, 184; Mays, 116–17; Wolff, 146; Wöhrle, Die frühen Sammlungen, 161.

55. Concerning the difficulties of 5:10(9), see the discussion of that verse below.

56. Utzschneider comes very close to articulating a similar position when he notes that the use of “this one” marks the point at which the direct address of the ruler in 5:1–3 changes to a third-person reference to the ruler (Utzschneider, “Micha und die Zeichen der Zeit,” 272).

57. See the discussion of this linkage below in the comments to 5:10(9).

58. See Prov 30:21–22, 29–31.

59. Typically, one associates positive motivations and actions on the part of the shepherd when one finds the term shepherd used with flock (e.g., Isa 40:11; Jer 23:2; 31:10; Mic 7:14) or “shepherd my people” (e.g., 2 Sam 7:7; 1 Chr 17:6; Jer 23:2).

60. Following the siege of Sennacherib in 701 BCE, Judah essentially became a vassal state to the Assyrians, especially during the lengthy fifty-five-year reign of Manasseh (698–644 BCE), even though Davidic kings remained on the throne. During the reign of Josiah, Assyria’s power waned in the region and Josiah moved toward greater autonomy, especially after the destruction of Nineveh in 612 BCE, but Josiah’s death in 609 BCE put an end to those hopes. See Miller and Hayes, History of Ancient Israel and Judah, 433–36, 449–50, 454–61.

61. Sweeney, 2:391–92. Jeremias (189–90) notes that 5:7(6) and 5:8(7) act as contrasting images to announce Yahweh’s blessings on the nations (5:7[6]) and his destructive power exerted upon them (5:8[7]). Micah 5:9[8], however, pronounces its judgment against those who have refused to see the remnant of Jacob as a blessing. As such it is an extension of both 5:7(6) and 5:8(7).

62. Wolff, 152–57.

63. Exod 7:11; Deut 18:10; 2 Kgs 9:22; 2 Chr 33:6; Isa 47:9, 12; Jer 27:9; Dan 2:2; Mic 5:11; Nah 3:4; Mal 3:5.

64. The polemical tone is also noteworthy in that narrative accounts associate this behavior with royal figures who are condemned for their syncretistic religious practices, namely Jezebel (2 Kgs 9:22) and Manasseh (2 Chr 33:6).

65. The condemnation of Jezebel (2 Kgs 9:22) represents the biggest exception, but she is such a polemical figure in her own right, it stands to reason she would be accused of virtually every sin imaginable.

66. Debate exists over whether ʿnn (“cloud”) represents the same root as the word for soothsaying, or whether it has a different etymology. David Noel Freedman and B. E. Willoughby, “עָנָן,” TDOT 11:253. The verbal forms of this verb also appear in polemical contexts: 2 Kgs 21:6 (= 2 Chr 33:6); Isa 2:6; 57:3; Jer 27:9.

67. See discussions of the difficulties in interpreting this and other divinatory terminology in the Old Testament in Joanne K. Kuemmerlin-McLean, “Magic: Old Testament,” ABD 4:468–71.

68. In this respect, see Deut 7:21, 25; 12:3; 2 Kgs 17:41; Ps 78:55–58.

69. See the functions of maṣṣēbôt described in Dale W. Manor, “Massebah,” ABD 4:602.

70. For a fuller discussion of the meaning of Asherah, see Baruch Margalit, “The Meaning and Significance of Asherah,” VT 40 (1990): 286–88, DOI: 10.2307/1519533. Margalit illustrates three primary meanings of Asherah in the Hebrew Bible: (1) as something organic that is planted; (2) as the name of a divine persona; and (3) as a shorthand reference to an idol. In the last category, which fits the context of Mic 5:13, Margalit lists 2 Kgs 21:3, 7 as textual support.

71. Most notably, see the discussion of the texts and the drawing from Kuntillet ʿAjrud (Margalit, “Asherah,” 274–78). See also the distinctions in gender and number made by Park in relation to Deuteronomy: “In summary, ʾašerâ, the singular form, is normally used everywhere, in a temple setting or at the high places, whereas ʿašerîm, the masculine plural form, always refers to the cult objects at the high places. The word ʾašerôt, the feminine plural form, indicates the cult objects which emphasize the femininity of the goddess in association with the male deity like Baal.” Sung Jin Park, “The Cultic Identity of Asherah in Deuteronomistic Ideology of Israel,” ZAW 123 (2011): 564, DOI: 10.1515/ZAW.2011.036. The Micah text corresponds to this pattern as well.

72. Whatever the precise physical form, Sweeney (2:393) is surely correct that the Asherim represent another form of idolatry, thereby referring back to 5:13(12) while the destruction of the cities summarizes the message of 4:9–10.

73. E.g., Wolff, 157–59; Sweeney, 2:392–93.

74. Steck, Theological Witness; van der Toorn, Scribal Culture and the Making of the Hebrew Bible; Carr, Writing on the Tablet of the Heart; and Carr, Formation of the Hebrew Bible.

75. Steck, Theological Witness. See esp. his discussion of “Book Signals for a Coherent Reading,” 34–43; and “The View of the Prophet in the Given Prophetic Book,” 43–52.
